newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sidesteps issue of Taleban recognition.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sidesteps issue of Taleban recognition.

text.p: The United States called on Tuesday for an end to fighting in Afghanistan but left unclear whether it would recognise the Taleban movement which has extended its control to most of the country in recent days.

The State Department urged creation of a "broadly representative government" in Afghanistan and told Taleban it would need to moderate its policies if it hoped to attract Western aid to rebuild the war-shattered country.

"The United States continues to urge an immediate end to fighting," spokesman John Dinger said as the Taleban Islamic militia battled rival forces in Mazar-i-Sharif, captured last weekend from opposition leader Gen. Abdul Rashid Dostum.
"We call on all Afghan parties to avoid violence, repression, or reprisals in the aftermath of the fall of General Dostum," Dinger told a news briefing.

"We also urge the Taleban and other Afghan groups to join together to establish a broadly representative government that will protect the rights of all Afghans and abide by Afghanistan's international obligations."
Dinger dodged questions on whether the United States planned to accept Taleban as the government of Afghanistan, saying that Washington "recognizes states, not governments."
But he acknowledged that the issue could come up if Taleban asked either to take control of the Afghan embassy in Washington or to take up Afghanistan's United Nations seat.

"Should that happen we will take an appropriate position," he said, adding that Washington had no plans to send an ambassador. The United States cleared all its diplomats out of Afghanistan in the late 1980s because of escalating violence.
Despite maintaining contacts with Taleban the United States has avoided getting too close to the movement, partly due to hostile U.S. media coverage of its tough restrictions on women.
"What Afghanistan is going to need in order to recover from the many years of war is international assistance, international engagement, international involvement," Dinger said.

"The Taleban should see it as being in its interest to adopt policies that are going to encourage international engagement. And I would think that an easing of the restrictions and activities of women and girls would certainly be one of those steps."
